name: Hexagonal pyramid
seoTitle: Hexagonal pyramid Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Hexagonal pyramid: work out base length (a) from the pyramid height and the base area. A free math calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Supply the pyramid height and the base area and the Hexagonal pyramid calculator solves for base length (a). Think of it as a shortcut for a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm. Change one value and the results step aside until you press Calculate again, which is what makes it easy to see how much the answer really depends on that one input.

sections.title: How does the Hexagonal pyramid calculator work?
sections.html:
The Hexagonal pyramid calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports base length (a) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the pyramid height (h) and the base area.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Hexagonal pyramid calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Base length (a)=(1 ÷ 3) × the square root of (2) × (3 ^ 1 ÷ 4) × the square root of (base area)
Face area=(1 ÷ 4) × base length (a) × the square root of (3 × (base length (a) ^ 2) + 4 × (pyramid height (h) ^ 2))
Face area=(1 ÷ 6) × lateral surface area
Total surface area=base area + lateral surface area
Base length (a)=(1 ÷ 3) × the square root of (2) × (3 ^ 3 ÷ 4) × the square root of (volume ÷ pyramid height (h))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Hexagonal pyramid calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value
  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Checking a homework answer before you hand it in
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the pyramid height and the base area — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Hexagonal pyramid calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns base length (a), derived from the pyramid height and the base area. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Hexagonal pyramid calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the pyramid height and the base area, which is 2 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter base length (a) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Base length (a) opens in millimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: Is the Hexagonal pyramid calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
